title: Expert workflows: Legal context becomes product infrastructure
desc: Turns tacit lawyer knowledge into bounded, evaluated services, potentially shifting delivery beyond time sales without eliminating hourly advice.

kps.k: The central proposition is that legal AI creates value by turning expert knowledge into integrated workflows, not merely by accelerating isolated tasks.
kps.d: Harvey’s founders describe combining reusable capabilities with matter documents, external authorities and client-specific practices. CoCounsel describes converting guidance into agentic workflows, while GC AI extends contract review and compliance analysis into communication and implementation. These accounts locate the product challenge in coordinating an entire process. Crosby’s Ryan Daniels adds that connecting automated segments to remaining human work requires difficult operational redesign. Reported capabilities and development plans do not establish reliable end-to-end autonomy.

qs.q: And so just thinking about the whole chain of what people do,  there's a lot of features there and our road map is all around basically extending that.
qs.a: Cecilia Ziniti — GC AI (Founder & CEO, former General Counsel) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: It's really hard to pick apart if you have a hundredstep workflow and you know step 17 through 30 you can push to automation and steps you know 36 through 41 like having to find the interplay to push to automation is an extremely complex task that I think you probably need like really smart operators to figure out.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

kps.k: Experienced lawyers supply product specifications, decision context and quality judgments that final legal documents alone do not capture.
kps.d: Weinberg distinguishes lawyers’ roles as design partners and evaluators, arguing that complex evaluation requires senior expertise. Pereyra identifies the reasoning behind transactional choices and partner corrections as potentially valuable training material absent from public filings. Crosby similarly emphasises lawyers and engineers using the product together to discover workflow gaps. The Olivia Dhein discussion qualifies the prospect of learning expert judgment: equally capable lawyers can reach opposing conclusions, so capturing decisions does not establish a single correct approach.

qs.q: And so you do see the final result, but most of the  >> value or what you need, I think, to  eventually improve these models is the decision-m process.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (No Priors Ep. 142) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: The challenge there I think though is that in a lot of legal situations, it is just a question of judgment and you could have two equally good lawyers who reach out entirely opposite views on things.
qs.a: Olivia Dhein: Lawyers, AI, And The New Non-Negotiable · Law firms · 2026

kps.k: Realistic legal evaluation is both a development bottleneck and a claimed source of competitive advantage.
kps.d: Pereyra contrasts readily checkable clause extraction with merger drafting that resists binary scoring. Harvey’s benchmark approach uses lawyer-specified synthetic matters, agent-generated documents and lawyer-reviewed rubrics; diligence checks test whether outputs identify materially important issues, not just provisions. This addresses confidential-data constraints but leaves substantial limits: initial synthetic drafts need review, detailed tests require practice-specific work, and synthetic task distributions do not match production use. Benchmark scores therefore do not establish production reliability or replace human verification before reliance.

qs.q: But for something like generate this merger agreement,  >> it's really hard to just give some  binary like this is good or this is bad.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey (No Priors Ep. 142) · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: We had agents generate the data from there and then we sent it to sort of like our larger uh, of lawyers  to review the outputs, the rubrics, document, uh, quality, all those sorts of things.
qs.a: Gabe Pereyra — Harvey: the legal agent benchmark and the coming token-pricing reckoning · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Open-ended experimentation discovers valuable uses, but deployable products need task-specific boundaries, controls and model selection.
kps.d: Supio reports lawyers extending question-answering into analysis and drafting, while warning that conversational freedom masks uneven capability. Harvey favours scoped workflows behind a simpler interface; Ironclad selects models according to the task, and David Wakeling seeks vendor portability. Reliability standards also vary: Wakeling compares diligence tools with material that otherwise goes unreviewed, whereas Ironclad’s Jason Boehmig stresses accurate authorities in case-law applications. Neither position supplies an achieved error rate. Agent access controls, confidentiality and privilege remain separate deployment requirements, not consequences of strong model performance.

qs.q: The the whole like trap of conversational AI is that you can literally ask anything and some things it's really good at answering and some things it's not.
qs.a: Ep 295: How One Mass Tort Firm Uses Supio, the AI Platform for PI Lawyers · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: in M&A due diligence, where you wouldn't have been able to review that volume of data to begin with 31:32  - How do you think about the buy vs build decision?** **32:18  In terms of the value chain, we have a foundational model, we then have Harvey leveraging and tuning it for law, and then at the far other end you have a human using this product; what fits in between the human and the model?
qs.a: Closing the Loop ep. 0012 — The law firm that's built a large and successful software business (David Wakeling, Allen & Overy) · Market & press · 2023

kps.k: Commercialising expertise could shift legal delivery from selling lawyer time toward software-enabled products, without eliminating hourly advice.
kps.d: Weinberg reports firms beginning to sell specialised Harvey systems and predicts software margins could improve discounted or loss-leading work while premium advice remains hourly. Legora’s Max Junestrand similarly envisages partners serving far more clients than an associate pyramid permits. Crosby takes a different route: it delivers legal services and bills by the document, requiring forecasts of the full negotiation workload. Its founders nevertheless accept hourly billing for sophisticated, unpredictable matters. These are distinct vendor-enabled and service-provider models, with pricing and profitability largely unproven in the supplied evidence.

qs.q: Instead of only being to work with my pyramid of associates, I'm a I'm now able to do work that I could scale to, you know, hundreds or thousands of clients at the same time.
qs.a: AI Driven Legal Evolution - Max Junestrand - Legora - Episode #64 · Legal-tech vendor · 2025

qs.q: guessed a year ago is being able to predict from time zero how long this piece of work is going to take so that we can price it and still you know make sure that we're doing the work properly that we align with the value that we're giving the clients and you know that's like where things get really interesting because you have to predict you know how many times will this contract go back and forth.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: The competitive divide concerns whether incumbent firms will capture these gains or lose work to redesigned providers and client self-service.
kps.d: Harvey and Eudia emphasise collaboration with incumbent partners, and Legora points to existing innovation teams. Daniels and General Legal’s Ryan Walker instead stress labour-based incentives, partnership interests and technical-capability gaps that may impede reform; Walker forecasts new firms rising through the AmLaw rankings. These positions differ in emphasis rather than establish mutually exclusive outcomes. Covenant’s Jen Berrent explicitly designs for fewer outside-counsel consultations, while the Axiom–Harvey discussion proposes allocating more work to in-house teams and flexible providers. Shared systems could therefore strengthen some firm relationships while reducing firms’ scope on individual matters.

qs.q: So we see technology like Harvey Share Spaces  as a way to finally unbundle some of that work  so that only the parts that need to go to the law firm  are actually going to the law firm.
qs.a: LawTech Talks: How AI is reshaping collaboration across the legal ecosystem — CJ Saretto (Axiom) & Ashleigh Whittaker (Harvey Australia) with Jerome Doraisamy (Lawyers Weekly) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: Buyer value includes usable knowledge, continuity and fewer handoffs—not only faster document production.
kps.d: Berrent advocates client-facing information interfaces and embedded advice rather than delivery ending with documents or emails. The Axiom–Harvey discussion proposes preserving diligence analysis, decision rationales and rerunnable workflows for acquisition integration. The SRA in-house panel highlights institutional knowledge, repository-based answers and risk-based escalation. These proposals imply designing around client decisions and business processes, with explicit ownership, access permissions and review thresholds. Technology-led delivery need not mean impersonal acquisition: Berrent reports that initial personal relationships remain central to trust.

qs.q: But the delivery of legal services could provide control over data and information to those clients in an interface that's technology that looks like any other SAS product that HR or finance would have.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on structure, conflicts and legal data in private markets · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: So my partner Richard Paris who's former general counsel of CBC Capital Partners or myself really meets with every client still even if after that initial meeting the human contact actually may drop off significantly.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on structure, conflicts and legal data in private markets · AI-native providers · 2026

kps.k: Claims of augmentation leave open how firms will develop expertise and how much work will remain with lawyers.
kps.d: Weinberg predicts task displacement and earlier strategic assignments rather than lawyer job loss. Pereyra reports educational use and proposes firm-specific curricula, while Ford’s in-house respondents favour shadowing and redesigned education over preserving routine work as training. These claims answer concerns about losing the associate learning pipeline but do not demonstrate improved learning or employment outcomes. Nor do they imply that AI is confined to junior work: Pereyra reports strategic uses, and Eudia aspires to higher-value matters while acknowledging that its model remains at an early proof stage.

qs.q: And so, so I mean, I think there's  there's actually kind of like um two steps and and we're we're at the beginning of proving step one, but I think step one is proving this actually works.
qs.a: Omar Haroun — Eudia: Outcomes, the Law-Firm Arm, and the In-House Bet for 2026 · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

kps.k: The evidence supports emerging practices and testable propositions more strongly than general claims of transformation.
kps.d: Most accounts come from founders, practitioners and sometimes investor interviewers, using demonstrations, estimates and customer anecdotes rather than independent outcome studies. Weinberg’s early test reports unanimous willingness among three specialists to send 86 of 100 answers without edits—not an independently established accuracy rate. Wakeling estimates a couple of hours saved weekly without a measurement method. Berrent reports self-service increasing from 55% to 90%, while expecting 80%, but supplies no sample size or year. Practice-specific ROI, durable competitive advantage and market reshuffling remain claims to evaluate. Likewise, reported court work and proposed consensual settlement assistance do not demonstrate access-to-justice gains.

qs.q: On 86 out of 100 of those questions, three out of three attorneys said yes.
qs.a: Winston Weinberg — Harvey (CEO) on Judgment Versus Routine Work, Lockstep Promotion and Why Legal Fees Haven't Fallen · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: 33:01  - We believe we save a couple hours per week; across 3.7k lawyers, that's a lot of hours of lawyers' time** **33:56  Thinking about the value chain is a nice starting point for where we go next...
qs.a: Closing the Loop ep. 0012 — The law firm that's built a large and successful software business (David Wakeling, Allen & Overy) · Market & press · 2023

vlens.an: The selected AI-native legal-provider sources accept the proposition that legal AI’s value comes from converting expert knowledge into bounded, integrated delivery systems rather than merely accelerating individual tasks. They materially extend it with operating models: Crosby joins lawyers and engineers to identify end-to-end workflow gaps, retains expert verification of quality and safety, and prices contract services by document; Covenant embeds lawyer-programmed commentary and verified transaction information into client-facing tools that support self-service and reduce outside-counsel handoffs. Common reasons include better alignment with client decisions, reuse of expertise that would otherwise remain in lawyers’ heads, and the need to redesign both workflows and commercial incentives. Material variation concerns where value is captured: Crosby emphasises provider-side contract execution and forecasting the full negotiation workload, Covenant emphasises client control over information and self-service while preserving relationship-based trust, and General Legal chiefly advances a forecast that AI-native firms will compete with established firms. The sources also differ in evidential strength: Covenant reports adoption figures, but without independent validation or sufficient methodological detail; Crosby’s efficiency expectations and General Legal’s predicted AmLaw reshuffle remain largely anecdotal or prospective. Accordingly, these curated sources develop the proposition through concrete service designs without establishing general market transformation or reliable end-to-end autonomy.

qs.q: It's actually using the product, experiencing it, doing user research and understanding what are the critical workflows, what are the biggest gaps and actually being able to, you know, recognize and say from start to finish like you know it's more than just a benchmark.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels & John Sarihan (Crosby) — Sequoia Training Data Ep.61 · AI-native providers · 2026

qs.q: All of that is verified and then they know that that AI level of commentary has been  programmed by a lawyer right like we're saying this is what's important that 90% of the time the clients could take it themselves to the finish line.
qs.a: Jen Berrent — Covenant (founder) on what makes a firm 'AI-first' · AI-native providers · 2025

vlens.an: The curated legal-tech vendor sources collectively accept the proposition that legal AI’s distinctive value lies in converting legal expertise, matter context and client-specific practices into bounded workflows rather than merely accelerating isolated tasks. They materially develop it with concrete mechanisms: reusable AI patterns and chained agents; lawyer-authored specifications and task-specific evaluation; synthetic, lawyer-reviewed benchmark matters; document-aware memory; practice-specific playbooks; workflow continuity across review, communication and implementation; and software-enabled commercialisation of firm expertise. Several also extend the buyer-side implications through matter unbundling, retained decision context and fewer handoffs. Material internal variation concerns scope and maturity, not the proposition’s core: some sources emphasise firm products and new pricing, others in-house contract or compliance workflows, training, small-claims processes or faster product development. Some envisage higher-value and strategic work, while others remain focused on bounded contract or research tasks. The more cautious accounts stress uneven open-ended performance, benchmark-to-production mismatch, difficult evaluation of complex drafting and lack of enterprise readiness; two sources are too thin to establish a clear position. Across the selection, commercial, reliability and access-to-justice claims are mostly forecasts, demonstrations or company and customer anecdotes rather than independent outcome evidence. This synthesis describes only the supplied curated vendor voices and should not be treated as representative of legal-tech vendors generally.

qs.q: Um I would say one big challenge, one of the biggest challenges so we can generate these very realistic synthetic data sets, we can augment them with humans, but the distribution of that data still doesn't match our production distribution.
qs.a: How Harvey Built a Research Lab on a Budget · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an: This curated set broadly accepts the proposition that legal AI creates value by translating legal expertise into bounded products and workflows rather than merely providing access to a general model. It materially develops that proposition by identifying specific enabling infrastructure: law-firm domain expertise translated into client-facing systems, vendor-portable product architecture, accumulated workflow data, legal-output evaluation frameworks, step-level evaluation for agentic systems, and security and permissioning controls. Common reasons include the need to embed legal context between the model and the human user, to tailor risk standards to particular use cases, and to commercialise repeatable expertise beyond conventional time-based delivery. Material variation concerns emphasis: one Harvey account stresses partner-led product commercialisation and adjacent-domain transfer; Wakeling focuses on use-case-relative risk and portability across vendors; another Harvey account treats workflow data and evaluation as competitive advantages while acknowledging that secure agent deployment remains unfinished. These sources provide qualitative observations, estimates and company claims rather than independent evidence of production reliability, profitability or market-wide transformation; their agreement should not be read as representative of market analysts, consultancies and press generally.

qs.q: You have to set up evaluation frameworks and agentic systems that can self-eval all the different steps.
qs.a: Inside Harvey: How a First-Year Legal Associate Built One of Silicon Valley's Hottest Startups · Market & press · 2025

vlens.an: The selected in-house counsel and legal-operations source supports the proposition, chiefly by rejecting the idea that legal work is too bespoke to be mapped into repeatable, AI-enabled workflows. It also accepts that AI may absorb routine junior work and argues that the response should be deliberate redesign of lawyer training—especially through shadowing and other forms of contextual learning—rather than preserving document review and processing as an implicit apprenticeship system. This aligns with the synthesis’s view that value comes from structuring expert knowledge and connecting automation to human judgment, while leaving strategic collaboration with lawyers in place. There is some internal variation in emphasis: the interviewer foregrounds risks to law-firm leverage and the future supply of strategic advisers, whereas the respondent is more confident that alternative training methods exist and challenges legal exceptionalism. The support remains experiential and prospective: the source refers to personal learning and workflow mapping but provides neither completed quantitative evidence nor proof of reliable end-to-end products, commercial outcomes or improved training. Because this is one curated source, its position should not be treated as representative of in-house counsel or legal operations generally.

This traditional-law-firm source supports the proposition that legal AI’s distinctive value can come from converting lawyers’ tacit decision processes into product infrastructure. It treats captured “decision traces”—such as clause selection, amendments and litigation choices—as a plausible basis for systems that mirror expert approaches, rather than merely accelerate isolated tasks. Its support is qualified in two material ways. First, the capability remains conditional rather than demonstrated: the discussion says such capture could produce an expert-like product, not that Harvey already reproduces expert judgment reliably. Second, legal judgment is not always reducible to a single correct workflow because equally capable lawyers may reasonably disagree. The source’s anecdotal first-level-review examples further support bounded, task-specific automation and expose weaknesses in traditional junior-heavy disclosure workflows, but they do not establish senior-level performance, end-to-end autonomy or the cluster’s broader commercial predictions. As this facet contains one curated source, these observations describe that source’s position rather than traditional law firms generally.

qs.q: And I think that if how good lawyers collectively thought could be captured, then yes, you could see why then you could end up with a product that was able to sort of mirror their approaches.
qs.a: Olivia Dhein: Lawyers, AI, And The New Non-Negotiable · Law firms · 2026

qs.q: The challenge there I think though is that in a lot of legal situations, it is just a question of judgment and you could have two equally good lawyers who reach out entirely opposite views on things.
qs.a: Olivia Dhein: Lawyers, AI, And The New Non-Negotiable · Law firms · 2026

vlens.an: The SRA in-house panel supports the proposition that legal AI creates value chiefly by embedding legal knowledge in bounded, integrated workflows rather than merely accelerating isolated tasks. Its examples connect research, contextualisation and drafting; institutionalise repeatable knowledge through repositories; and use risk-based escalation so routine outputs can proceed while higher-risk matters receive human review. The panel also aligns with the proposition’s emphasis on continuity, fewer legal queues and explicit controls around permissions, privilege, confidentiality and data. Internal variation concerns implementation rather than the core proposition: speakers range from simple drafting and intake automation to predictions of more agentic workflows, while stressing problem-led scoping, organisational leadership and differing regulatory or operational conditions. Claims about future agent growth and faster in-house adoption are experience-based and not supported by comparative outcome data, so the source supports emerging practices more clearly than broad transformation or reliable autonomy. This assessment concerns this curated panel only and does not establish the prevalence of these views among regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources consistently support the proposition that generative legal AI creates value when specialised legal knowledge is embedded in bounded products and workflows, rather than used only for generic task acceleration. Common reasons include tailoring systems to legal context, selecting models according to distinct task requirements, integrating AI across contract workflows, and placing product infrastructure between foundation models and human users. They also support the synthesis’s caution: reported benefits are primarily ambitions, strategic judgments, personal experience and unverified estimates, not evidence of reliable end-to-end autonomy, sustained cost reduction or market-wide transformation. Material variation concerns emphasis rather than direction. Robin AI stresses specialised contract intelligence and longer-term cost and access ambitions; Ironclad focuses on task-specific model selection, contract expertise, data and use-case-dependent reliability; Wakeling emphasises product packaging, use-case-relative risk and vendor portability; and the Ford in-house respondents focus on redesigning junior-lawyer training as routine work changes. The latter develops the workforce implications but does not redirect the core product-infrastructure proposition. Because these are curated sources, their alignment should not be read as measuring the prevalence of these views among vendors, firms or in-house counsel generally.

qs.q: how do we package / build products around the LLM to provide value?

elens.an: Across this curated set of 2025 sources, the evidence accepts the synthesis’s principal proposition and materially develops it with concrete accounts of adoption at scale. The common reasoning is that useful legal AI depends on combining reusable capabilities with matter context, firm or client knowledge, expert-designed steps, evaluation, permissions and human review across an integrated process—not merely giving lawyers a general-purpose assistant. Sources describe practice-specific workflows, institutional knowledge repositories, lawyer-programmed client outputs, matter-level agents and specialised systems that can commercialise expertise or enable self-service. They also identify material conditions for scaling: senior-lawyer participation in design and evaluation, operational work to reconnect automated and human steps, partner or leadership sponsorship, simple interfaces, risk-based escalation and access controls. Internal variation concerns where the resulting value accrues. Harvey and Legora accounts emphasise incumbent firms scaling or selling expertise while retaining premium hourly advice; Covenant anticipates fewer outside-counsel consultations; in-house speakers focus on continuity, consistency and reducing routine legal queues. Some sources frame AI as augmentation and earlier access to strategic work, while others foresee reduced human work per transaction. Confidence also varies: reported customer use and product practices provide evidence of emerging adoption, but forecasts of software-scale delivery, ROI and market transformation are generally based on founder experience, analogy or anecdotes rather than independent outcome studies. Security, complex-output evaluation and workflow integration remain unfinished constraints. The Norm Ai excerpt is compatible with augmentation but too nonspecific to establish how expert knowledge becomes workflow infrastructure; it does not materially alter the overall direction of this curated evidence.

qs.q: It's really hard to pick apart if you have a hundredstep workflow and you know step 17 through 30 you can push to automation and steps you know 36 through 41 like having to find the interplay to push to automation is an extremely complex task that I think you probably need like really smart operators to figure out.
qs.a: Ryan Daniels — Crosby (AI-native law firm) · AI-native providers · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 sources accept the proposition’s core and materially develop it through concrete accounts of how expert legal knowledge can become product and service infrastructure. They describe lawyer–engineer collaboration to identify end-to-end workflows; lawyer-informed synthetic matters, rubrics and legal unit tests for evaluation; document-aware memory and rapid translation of product requirements into software; client-facing data interfaces; reusable diligence workflows; and document-priced contract services combining AI with expert verification. Buyer-side sources further extend the proposition from production efficiency to continuity of knowledge, fewer handoffs and allocation of work among in-house teams, law firms and flexible providers. Material variation concerns the institutional form and maturity of these models: some sources envisage collaboration with incumbent firms, while others predict AI-native providers competing directly with them; some focus on bounded contract or diligence workflows, while others explore higher-value work, small-claims filing or consensual settlement. The commercial models likewise range from software-enabled firm systems to AI-native legal-service providers, while retaining hourly billing for sophisticated, unpredictable advice. Across these curated sources, demonstrations, founder accounts, informal adoption reports and forecasts are more common than independent outcome evidence. Synthetic evaluations may not match production use, complex contexts remain difficult, and several claimed market or service transformations are explicitly prospective. Two adjacent sources establish only limited usefulness, enterprise immaturity or barriers to reform and therefore do not clearly address the central workflow proposition; none of the supplied evidence clearly rejects it.
